DOCUMENT:
Vendor Comparison: Payroll and HR System Replacement
Ostrander Facilities Services Ltd, Systems Project Board paper, June 2026

1. Background
Ostrander employs 1,450 people, most of them hourly-paid cleaning and security staff working across around 300 client sites, paid weekly, with a smaller salaried population paid monthly. Our current payroll system reaches end of support in December 2027. Payroll errors are a persistent problem: in 2025 we made 2,140 corrections, mostly arising from late or incorrect timesheet data, and each correction costs around £18 in payroll staff time.

A formal tender was issued in February 2026. Six responses were received and three suppliers were shortlisted: PayNorth, Clearledger and Stafflow. Each gave a scripted demonstration using our own pay rules, and we took up two or three customer references for each.

2. Evaluation criteria
Bids were scored against four weighted criteria agreed by the Board before the tender: functionality (40 points), three-year cost (30 points), implementation and support (20 points) and customer references (10 points). Cost points were awarded in proportion to the lowest three-year cost.

3. Costs
Licence prices are per-employee-per-month quotes applied to our headcount of 1,250. Implementation covers configuration, data migration, parallel running and training.

Table 1. Three-year cost of ownership
Vendor | Implementation (one-off) | Annual licence | Three-year total
PayNorth | £68,000 | £54,000 | £212,000
Clearledger | £42,000 | £61,000 | £225,000
Stafflow | £95,000 | £47,000 | £236,000

PayNorth offers the lowest three-year cost, followed by Clearledger and then Stafflow, whose low licence fee is offset by the most expensive implementation.

4. Functionality
All three systems handle weekly and monthly payrolls, statutory reporting and pension auto-enrolment. Stafflow scored highest on functionality because of its rostering module, although we would not use this initially. PayNorth scored strongly for its mobile timesheet app and its automated validation rules, which flag missing or implausible hours before a pay run. Clearledger's timesheet integration requires a third-party add-on.

5. References
PayNorth's three reference customers reported that payroll error rates fell by an average of 40% in the first year after go-live. This demonstrates that PayNorth's automated validation rules substantially reduce errors, and on our 2025 volumes a 40% reduction would avoid around 856 corrections a year, worth roughly £15,400. All three reference customers implemented PayNorth as part of a wider payroll transformation that also moved them from paper to electronic timesheets and retrained their payroll teams.

Clearledger's references were positive about the product but two of three reported implementation overruns of more than three months. Stafflow's references were satisfied overall but described the support desk as slow.

6. Scores
Table 2. Weighted evaluation scores
Vendor | Functionality (40) | Cost (30) | Implementation and support (20) | References (10) | Total (100)
PayNorth | 34 | 30 | 16 | 9 | 89
Clearledger | 31 | 28 | 17 | 7 | 83
Stafflow | 35 | 27 | 13 | 8 | 83

7. Implementation plan
PayNorth proposes a nine-month implementation, with go-live for the April 2027 tax year and three months of parallel running before that. This leaves eight months of contingency before our current system's end of support. We will need to second two payroll officers to the project for the duration, backfilled from the project budget.

8. Recommendation
PayNorth is the highest-scoring bidder by a clear margin of six points. It offers the lowest three-year cost, strong functionality in the area that matters most to us, timesheet capture, and reference evidence that its software materially reduces payroll errors. We recommend that the Board approve contract award to PayNorth for an initial three-year term, at a total cost of £212,000.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "PayNorth | £68,000 | £54,000 | £212,000" -- PayNorth's three-year total should be £68,000 + 3 x £54,000 = £230,000, not £212,000. Correctly computed, Clearledger (£225,000) is cheapest, so PayNorth should not receive full cost points and the 'lowest three-year cost' claim and recommended contract value are wrong.
2. [inconsistency] at: "Licence prices are per-employee-per-month quotes applied to our headcount of 1,250." -- The Background states Ostrander employs 1,450 people, but licence costs are calculated on a headcount of 1,250. The headcount contradicts itself, and the licence costs are understated if 1,450 is correct.
3. [unsupported_causal] at: "This demonstrates that PayNorth's automated validation rules substantially reduce errors" -- The 40% fall is a before/after change at reference sites that, as the document itself states, simultaneously moved from paper to electronic timesheets and retrained payroll teams. The improvement cannot be attributed to PayNorth's validation rules (and reference customers are vendor-selected).

REVIEW:
# Review: Payroll and HR System Vendor Comparison

The weighting agreed in advance, the scripted demos and the references give the process a solid base. But the paper has an arithmetic error that changes its main cost claim, and the errors-reduction argument goes further than the evidence allows. PayNorth probably still comes out ahead, but by a smaller margin and for different reasons than the paper gives. Both need fixing before the Board sees it.

## 1. PayNorth's three-year total is wrong, and it is not the cheapest bid

Table 1 gives PayNorth £68,000 implementation plus £54,000 a year. Over three years that is **£230,000**, not £212,000. The other two rows add up correctly (Clearledger £225,000, Stafflow £236,000).

With the corrected figure, the cost ranking becomes:

| Vendor | Three-year total | Rank |
|---|---|---|
| Clearledger | £225,000 | 1 |
| PayNorth | £230,000 | 2 |
| Stafflow | £236,000 | 3 |

This affects:
- **"Lowest three-year cost"** in §3, §8 and your summary. This claim no longer holds.
- **Cost scores.** Using your proportional method, Clearledger scores 30.0, PayNorth 29.3 and Stafflow 28.6.
- **Totals.** PayNorth 88.3, Clearledger 85.0, Stafflow 84.6. PayNorth still wins, but by about **3 points, not 6**.
- **The recommended contract value** of £212,000 in §8, which would be put to the Board £18,000 short.

## 2. The licence costs use the wrong headcount

§1 says Ostrander employs **1,450** people. §3 prices the licences on **1,250**. If licences are per employee paid, every annual licence figure is about 16% too low. On 1,450 heads:

| Vendor | Annual licence | Three-year total |
|---|---|---|
| Clearledger | ~£70,760 | ~£254,300 |
| PayNorth | ~£62,640 | ~£255,900 |
| Stafflow | ~£54,520 | ~£258,600 |

The ranking barely moves and PayNorth still leads by about 3 points. However, every total rises by roughly £25,000–£30,000, and the contract value the Board approves would be significantly understated. Either explain why 1,250 is the right billable number (for example, leavers or inactive records) or reprice on 1,450. Also confirm whether the quotes include annual price increases.

## 3. The 40% error reduction can't be credited to PayNorth's software

§5 says the reference results "demonstrate" that PayNorth's validation rules substantially reduce errors. The same paragraph then notes that all three reference customers also:
- moved from paper to electronic timesheets, and
- retrained their payroll teams.

Those changes could plausibly explain much or all of the 40% drop. The evidence fits "a wider payroll transformation reduced errors". It does not isolate the software. Other points to consider:
- The sample is three customers, chosen by the vendor.
- The paper doesn't say whether Ostrander already uses electronic timesheets. If it does, the biggest driver of the reference improvement may not apply to you.
- Your main error source is *late* timesheet data. Validation rules catch implausible hours but don't make site supervisors submit on time.

I'd present the £15,400 as an upper-bound illustration, not an expected benefit. I'd also drop "demonstrates" and "materially reduces" from §5 and §8. The arithmetic itself is correct (856 corrections × £18).

## 4. "Wins on the things that matter most" overstates the scores

On the corrected figures, PayNorth does not top functionality (Stafflow 35 vs 34), implementation and support (Clearledger 17 vs 16), or cost (Clearledger). It leads only on references, and it wins overall by being consistently strong across all four criteria. That is a perfectly good basis for an award, and the paper should say so honestly.

Two related points:
- Stafflow's functionality lead rests on a rostering module you don't plan to use. That's worth noting, though it doesn't change the result.
- Confirm whether Clearledger's price includes the third-party timesheet add-on. If not, its cost advantage may disappear.

## 5. The contingency is narrower than "eight months" suggests

Going live in April 2027 does leave about eight months before end of support in December 2027. But payroll go-lives are normally timed for the start of a tax year, and the next one (April 2028) falls after end of support. If April 2027 slips, the fallback is a mid-year go-live, which is more complex because year-to-date figures must be migrated. The Board should know that the real contingency is "one mid-year attempt", not eight free months.

Timing also matters. The paper is dated June 2026, and a nine-month plan only reaches April 2027 if work starts around July 2026. If the award has slipped since then, recheck the dates.

## Suggested changes

1. Correct PayNorth's total to £230,000 (or the repriced figure) and recompute Table 2.
2. Reconcile the headcount and state the contract value the Board is actually approving.
3. Reword §5 and §8 to treat the error reduction as indicative, not demonstrated.
4. Restate the recommendation as "highest overall score, by about 3 points, strongest on references and close on cost".
5. Add a sentence on the tax-year timing risk.

These fixes should still support awarding to PayNorth. They make the case smaller, but it is one the Board can rely on.
